claims.statement: Hatshepsut was a daughter of the king Thutmose I and became the chief queen of Thutmose II.

After the death of Thutmose II she acted as guardian and regent for the young Thutmose III, her nephew and stepson; by his seventh regnal year she had taken the public role of a king, while still referred to with feminine forms.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her modern role as the head of a large public authority.

claims.statement: She claimed to have been born of a union between her mother and the god Amun-Ra, and looked to her father Thutmose I as the source of her kingship.

Her dates follow different chronologies: The Metropolitan Museum of Art dates objects of her joint reign with Thutmose III to about 1473 to 1458 BCE, and the British Museum gives her dates as 1479 to 1457 BC. She died in the twenty-second regnal year of Thutmose III.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Dates are approximate; the record uses about 1458 BC for her death.

claims.statement: Her birth year is not recorded. An age of about 50 at death, suggested by study of the mummy identified as hers, would place her birth about 1507 BC; this is a rough estimate.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Used only to set an approximate, very uncertain birth year.

claims.statement: No earlier than the forty-second year of Thutmose III, at least twenty years after her death, a program began to efface and recarve her monuments.

In 2007 Zahi Hawass announced that KV60A, the mummy of an obese woman left on the floor of tomb KV60 in the Valley of the Kings, was Hatshepsut. The identification rested on CT scans, above all on a molar found in a small chest inscribed with her name from the royal cache DB320, which fitted a gap in KV60A's jaw where only one root of a molar remained.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents the announcement and its basis, not the identity itself.

claims.statement: The identification is debated: any link between these mummies and the inscribed chest is uncertain, the consensus cited is that the tooth probably broke after death rather than being extracted in life, the DNA results were preliminary, and identifications of royal mummies of this dynasty are often unclear.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Every finding on KV60A may not be hers.

claims.statement: The CT scans of KV60A were reported to show a woman of about 50, about five feet tall and greatly overweight, with severe dental disease (missing teeth, root remnants, bone eroded at root tips by infection, and severe gum disease), and osteoarthritis and osteoporosis; a burst abscess with spreading infection was suggested as a cause of death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Findings on remains whose identity is debated, reported in a magazine and a documentary fact sheet rather than a peer-reviewed paper. Not linked to the modern episode, which is set before her death.

claims.statement: A lesion in the left iliac bone of KV60A was read by the radiologist Ashraf Selim as more likely a metastatic deposit from another cancer than a primary bone tumour, which could not be totally excluded.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective; no cancer is diagnosed in the modern episode.

claims.statement: Diabetes has been proposed for KV60A on circumstantial grounds; the radiologist called it a theory that cannot be confirmed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective; the modern diabetes is a synthetic screening finding, not linked to this claim.

claims.statement: In 2011 the University of Bonn reported that a flask in its Egyptian Museum inscribed with her name held the dried residue of a skin lotion or medication (palm oil, nutmeg apple oil, unsaturated fatty acids and hydrocarbons from creosote and asphalt), including benzo(a)pyrene, a strong carcinogen, and suggested that she may have exposed herself to it over years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A hypothesis from a press release; no study is cited, and the flask's use by her is inferred.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Care for a 48-year-old woman with a painful swollen jaw from a dental abscess, and type 2 diabetes found on screening, as current guidance advises and without weight stigma: recognize the warning signs of spreading odontogenic infection; give an NSAID with acetaminophen for dental pain and no opioid; withhold antibiotics when the abscess is localized, there is no systemic involvement and definitive treatment is available the next day (ADA 2019); arrange urgent drainage and extraction; diagnose diabetes from two abnormal results in one sample; start metformin, then add a GLP-1 receptor agonist chosen for weight and glucose (ADA Standards of Care 2026), with an SGLT2 inhibitor not indicated without kidney or heart disease; start a statin as the Standards advise for adults 40 to 75 with diabetes; screen for eye, foot and kidney complications; explain the two-way link between periodontitis and diabetes and arrange periodontal therapy; manage knee osteoarthritis with exercise and a topical NSAID; and keep up cancer screening by age (mammography, colorectal and cervical) and bone health, without a search for bone cancer when nothing in the modern episode points to one. The modern episode is a teaching case, not a claim about her real illnesses, which cannot be known from ancient remains whose identity is debated.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Hatshepsut returns the day after her first visit. This morning Dr. Lindqvist-Bello of oral and maxillofacial surgery examined her, took a panoramic radiograph, drained the abscess and extracted the broken lower left molar under local anesthesia. The throbbing has eased since the drainage, and the swelling has not spread. She has had no fever, trouble opening her mouth, or trouble swallowing. She took ibuprofen and acetaminophen overnight as advised. She took her first metformin tablet with last night's meal without stomach upset. She has not checked her glucose at home.

interventions.display: Cancer screening by age: screening mammography (every two years from 40), fecal immunochemical test yearly or colonoscopy (from 45), and primary HPV testing every five years (30 to 65); no search for bone cancer, because nothing in her history, examination or blood tests points to one; bone health through weight-bearing and strengthening exercise, calcium from food and adequate vitamin D, with bone density testing at 65 or sooner if a risk factor appears

provenance_review.notes: Dorman's Oriental Institute essay, a Metropolitan Museum of Art collection record, a British Museum newsletter, the Archaeology magazine report on KV60A, the 2016 review of royal mummy identifications (abstract) and the University of Bonn press release logged. No peer-reviewed paper on the KV60A CT findings was found; the Met and Smithsonian essays could not be fetched.

safe_messaging_review.notes: Findings on the mummy are graded R because the identification is debated. Weight is discussed in person-first language and only with her permission. Ancient Egyptian culture is described plainly, without exoticizing.
